title: Dendritic copper microstructured electrodeposits for efficient and selective electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide into C1 and C2 hydrocarbons
abstract: Here, we report synthesis of copper microstructures-based electro-catalyst with controlled morphologies and crystallinity via a rudimentary simple and green electrochemical dissolution method. The variations in the growth pattern of the dendritic shaped Cu microstructures were studied to understand the evolution of Cu dendrites with respect to several electrolysis parameters viz. applied bias voltage, concentration of organic additives, i.e. L-ascorbic acid, and electrolysis time and temperature. We show that these microstructures demonstrate efficient and selective electrochemical conversion of CO2 into CO along with methane and ethane from CO2-saturated moistened di-methyl sulfoxide (DMSO) electrolyte solution. Our results establish that the selectivity for C1 or C2 hydrocarbons (methane or ethane) as a major product can be tuned systematically by altering the extent of branching in dendrite microstructures as well as the extent of exposure of (111) and (200) facets. The production of C1 and C2 hydrocarbons along with CO in the present study can be ascribed to the availability of protons from the residual water (< 0.2 % v/v or ca. 1000 ppm) in hygroscopic DMSO. The optimized dendritic shaped electro-catalyst is perceived to have the fine branching and exposed facets that convert CO2 into CO with Faradaic Efficiency (F.E.) of 32 %, ethane with F.E. of 29 % and methane with F.E. of 5%. The production of ethane reaches a maximum of 33 % at -1.5 V (NHE), which to the best of our knowledge is the highest reported so far for electroreduction of CO2 over Cu in organic media.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Growing energy demands and negative impacts on the environment has called for eco-friendly energy transduction and storage [1–4]. Capture and conversion of CO2 into value-added chemical feedstock such as fuels is proving to be one of the most required nails in addressing this growing issue [5–7]. Especially, conversion of CO2 to high energy density hydrocarbons such as methane and ethane that are compatible with the existing infrastructure has the potential to substitute the fossil fuels with an immediate effect [8–10]. Amongst different conversion routes, electrochemical method has shown great promise and potential to be the basis of a practical approach for CO2 utilization. It has the advantages that it can utilize excess energy from intermittent renewable sources in lieu of large-scale energy storage [7,11,12]. Amid the several materials explored in this pursuit, the metallic Cu-surfaces have demonstrated the best possibilities of electrocatalytic CO2 conversion into hydrocarbons in appreciable quantities [13–15]. Yet, the selectivity and the efficiency of Cu-based electrodes are not sufficient to make this process viable on an industrial scale.
Thus, the development of more efficient and selective electro-catalysts for catalyzing an electrochemical conversion of CO2 into hydrocarbons is one of the prime research activities in this regard.
Ordinarily, the rough surfaces have large surface area and prove better than the traditionally used smooth surfaces for electro-catalysis, including electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECO2R) [16–30]. For example, Lu et al. [20] have shown that porous Ag-nanostructures with enlarged surface area and the curved internal surfaces generate a large number of highly active step sites and impart exceptionally high ECO2R activity that is over 3000 times higher than that of the smooth polycrystalline counterpart at a moderate overpotential. Rosen et al. [21] demonstrated around 3-fold higher faradaic efficiency for the transformation of CO2 into CO on Zn-nanodendrites as compared to the bulk Zn-counterparts. Also, Tang et al. [22] have demonstrated that the roughened Cu-electrode surfaces (e.g. covered with Cu-nanoparticles or sputtered surfaces) exhibit better selectivity towards hydrocarbons compared with the electro-polished polycrystalline Cu-electrodes. These studies that very well establish a close correlation of the size, shape and morphology of metal nanostructures with their properties and hence applications underline the importance of designing the electrodes modified with high surface area nanostructures.
Among various specific nanostructures, dendritic materials with a self-assembled hierarchical structure consisting of a central stem and many side branches are fascinating both for fundamental studies and for potential applications in catalysis and other fields [31–34]. To date, several synthesis methods based on physical and solution-phase chemical routes have been developed for fabrication of dendritic metal nanostructures including Cu-nanodendrites. However, for most of these cases, the synthesis requires the presence of additional shape-directing agents like surfactants, polymers, and templates that ultimately limits their electrocatalytic activity. Alternatively, electro-deposition has been demonstrated to be a better strategy for the one-step, high yield synthesis of hierarchical metal micro/nanostructures where the morphology and/or structure of deposits can be controlled by adjusting the preparation conditions. Particularly, Liu and co-workers [35] prepared Cu-dendrites by electro-deposition in constant current mode, applying current density as high as 3 Acm−2. Popov et al. [36] reported the electro-deposition of Cu from CuSO4 electrolyte bath solution containing 0.5 M H2SO4. However, the potential of Cu-nanodendrites with high surface area in electro-catalytic applications has not been studied enough, specifically, towards the electrochemical transformation of CO2. It is pertinent to mention here that the use of surfactants/templates and stringent conditions such as highly acidic electrolyte medium with additives like sulfuric acid, phosphoric acid along with high temperature and voltages is common in the process of electro-deposition. Therefore, a template/surfactant-free electro-deposition route with mild experimental conditions for Cu-nanodendrites that can be easily adapted for the preparation of other nanostructures is highly desirable. Furthermore, the effect of electro-deposition parameters on the growth mechanism needs to be clarified and similarly study of the electro-catalytic activity of the as-prepared Cu-nanodendrites is essential.
Furthermore, most of the literature-reported studies towards the use of other shapes of Cu-nanostructures for efficient and selective ECO2R have used serious instrumentation and tedious sample preparation protocols [15,22,27,28,30]. For example, Cu-electrodes showing F.E. of ∼45 % for CO at an overpotential of ∼390mV were prepared by annealing Cu foil in the air at 500 °C for 12 h [15]. Similarly, Cu nanowire arrays demonstrating F.E. of ∼50 % for CO and less than 3% for ethane were prepared by annealing pre-formed Cu (OH)2 film (obtained by immersing Cu foil into a solution mixture containing ammonium persulfate and 2.7M NaOH) at 150 °C for 2 h [30]. Recently, Kea et al. [27] reported the F.E. of only ∼10 % for ECO2R to ethane at an applied potential of -0.9 V vs NHE using Cu-oxide derived Cu-electrodes comprised of nanoporous ribbon arrays, which to the best of our knowledge is the maximum F.E. value reported, so far. Earlier, Tang et al. [22] have obtained F.E. of ∼8% towards methane on Cu-sputtered on Cuplate electrodes along with trace quantities of ethane (F.E. < 2%). Sen et al. [28] also reported the formation of methane and ethane as minor products with F.E. of less than 2% on copper foams with hierarchical porosity obtained through galvanostatic (3 Acm−2) deposition of Cu on Cu plates from an electrolyte solution bath containing 1.5M sulfuric acid and 0.20M copper sulphate. Overall, there is an urgent need to design, develop and fabricate low-cost electro-catalyst materials for efficient conversion of CO2 into hydrocarbons. Notably, the F.E. reported so far for electrochemical conversion of CO2 to C1 and C2, high energy density hydrocarbons such as methane and ethane are remarkably low.
The Major cause of poor selectivity of Cu-surfaces for ECO2R to hydrocarbons in previous studies could be the use of aqueous solutions as an electrolyte medium in these investigations. This is becuase the
availability of protons in aqueous media during ECO2R facilitates the generation of products including CO and formic acid. Besides, competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) that takes place in the same potential range as that of ECO2R further lowers the FE for ECO2R. The lower solubility of CO2 in water is an addittional concern that limits the efficiency of ECO2R [37]. Therefore, the use of aprotic medium like organic solvents with more negative cathodic background limit of its potential window compared to water and no competitive HER along with higher solubility for CO2 (e.g. the solubility of CO2 in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) is 4.2 times than in water) would be beneficial for ECO2R [38]. However, it is a well-known fact that as a consequence of different CO2 activation pathways possible in organic solvents, ECO2R in these solvents generates CO as the major product along with carbonates and oxalates in minor quantities. However, an alternative pathway involving CO2•− protonation by residual water (in organic solvents) followed by electron transfer (since CO2•− is a possible source of electrons) leads to the formation of formate and hydrocarbons [39]. Thus, the use of organic solvents with the residual water would conceivably arouse the additional exploration of the prospects associated with this process of high environmental impact.
In this regard, we present a simple rudimentary process for electrode fabrication using Cu-nanodendrite assembly for selective electrochemical conversion of CO2 into hydrocarbons. Cu-nanodendrite microstructures were prepared by following a single-step DC electrophoretic dissolution/deposition method. The reaction parameters viz. applied bias voltage, concentration of the additives (i.e. ascorbic acid) and electrolysis time and temperature were optimized. Fascinatingly, the morphology and crystallinity of the Cu-electrodeposits that are controlled as a function of synthesis parameters are found to have a strong correlation with their electro-catalytic activity. Ascorbic acid (AscH2) has been chosen as an additive considering its excellent ability to donate electrons that makes (AscH−) an excellent reducing agent and antioxidant [40–42].

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials and chemicals
sections.text: All chemicals used in this study were of analytical grade. A Copper metal rod (99.9 % pure, metal basis) was procured from Alfa Aesar. Ascorbic acid (99 %) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (HPLC grade, water content: < 0.2 %) were procured from fisher scientific and used as received without further purification. Tetra-butyl ammonium tetrafluoroborate (TBABF4, 99 %) procured from Sigma Aldrich was dried in a vacuum oven at 80 °C and stored under vacuum desiccator before using it for the electrochemical measurements. Ultrapure CO2 and N2 gases were procured from Sigma Gases, New Delhi and before using were passed through a filter equipped with an oxygen trap, gas purifier and moisture trap to remove the traces of impurities and moisture (Prama Instruments Pvt. Ltd. India).

sections.heading: 2.2. Synthesis of dendritic Cu NPs
sections.text:
The dendritic Cu-nanostructures were prepared by following a modified DC electrophoresis method that we recently reported for the synthesis of plasmonic Cu/Cu-oxide nanostructures with varying shapes and morphologies [43]. Importantly, unlike similar DC electrophoreticdissolution/deposition methods reported in the literature, no harsh and stringent variables were employed in the present synthesis. Typically, a copper rod with 6mm diameter (sacrificial anode) was first cleaned in 0.1 M HNO3 and rinsed thoroughly with deionised water. A platinum wire loop with 2mm diameter (deposition substrate cathode) was cleaned in 0.1 M HCl for 20 s and then rinsed thoroughly with water. Keithley 2231A-30-3 triple channel DC power supply from Tektronix Inc. USA that can be operated under constant voltage or current was used as a voltage source. The positive terminal was connected to copper
rod whereas negative terminal was connected to Pt wire loop cathode immersed in a conventional glass electrochemical cell containing ascorbic acid solution in water and DC voltage was applied for the stipulated time interval. With time, the colour of the solution changes from colourless to pale blue (cyan) initially then to reddish brown suggesting the dissolution of metallic copper as copper ions into electrolyte solution followed by nucleation and growth of Cu-microstructures. Accumulation of a brownish mass of copper particles at the Pt cathode was also observed at a later part of the electrolysis. The obtained suspension was collected, centrifuged for 10min, washed with Milli-Q water several times followed by ethanol and then dried in a petri dish under vacuum at 50 °C for ca. 3 h. Several samples were prepared following the similar approach but varying the electrolysis parameters viz. applied voltage, L-ascorbic acid additive concentration, electrolysis time and temperature, one at a time. Based on the parameter of impact under consideration, four different batches of the deposits, with operations employed tabulated in Table SI-1 and described briefly as below were prepared.
Set I (Change in additive concentration): In this set, 40mL of electrolysis bath with varying concentrations of ascorbic acid viz. 25 mM, 75mM and 100mM was used while keeping other parameters constant such as temperature (80 °C), time (60min), stirring rate (600 rpm) and a bias voltage (30 V). The obtained samples were labelled as 25mM, 75mM and 100mM, respectively.
Set II (Applied DC voltage): After the comparative analysis of the shapes and morphologies of obtained materials from Set-I, 100mM concentration of ascorbic acid was found to be the most suitable for extended fractal dimension of dendrites and efficient ECO2R. Hence, in this set, the concentration of ascorbic acid was fixed to 100mM and applied DC voltage was varied viz. 7.5 V, 15 V and 30 V. The remaining parameters were fixed as per Set-I.
Set III (Electrodeposition temperature): In this set, electrodeposition temperature was varied as 60 °C, 70 °C, 80 °C and 90 °C while keeping ascorbic acid concentration to 100mM and a bias voltage of 30 V and electrodeposition duration of ca. 60min. The samples were collected as stated earlier and labelled as 60 °C, 70 °C, 80 °C and 90 °C, respectively.
Set IV (Electrodeposition duration): Finally, to study the evolution of dendrites and its effect on ECO2R, samples were collected at different time intervals viz. 10, 15, 30, 40, 45 and 60min, while keeping other parameters fixed.

sections.heading: 2.3. Material characterization
sections.text:
Crystallinity and lattice parameters of the prepared materials were analysed by recording powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) pattern using Bruker D8 Advance powder X-ray diffractometer with Cu Kα (λ=1.54 Å) radiation as an excitation source at a scan speed of 0.2 s/increment between 2θ values of 10° to 95°. The field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM) attached with Oxford-EDS system IE 250X max 80 with latest 80 mm2 SDD detector model FEI Quanta 200 were used to determine morphology and elemental composition of the as prepared materials by recording FESEM images and EDX spectra. Further, to confirm the microstructures, Technai transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging was also used for which a certain amount of sample dispersed in ethanol by sonicating for ca. 30 min was drop casted (ca. 5 μL) on carbon coated copper grid, and the prepared grid was dried well before recording the TEM images. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were carried over hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HAXPES) beamline BL-14, Indus-2 with double-crystal monochromator [Si (111)] and excitation energy of 4.311 keV. The system is equipped with hemispherical analyser and detector system (Phoibos 225, Specs make). The typical pressure in the experimental station is 5× 10−9 mbar. The survey spectra were recorded over a range of 0–1000 eV for each composition and energy calibration was done with respect to the reference (C1s peak at a binding energy value
of 284.8 eV adventitious carbon) for all edges.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
All the electrochemical measurements were performed using Metrohm Autolab PGSTAT-302 N potentiostat/galvanostat and an airtight electrochemical cell equipped with Cu-microstructures modified glassy carbon electrode (GCE) as working electrode, Ag/AgCl/saturated KCl as a reference electrode and platinum wire loop as a counter electrode. It is pertinent to mention here that since halogens are known to affect CO2 catalysis especially on copper substrates, we employed a gel-based reference electrolyte (Metrohm) as an ionically conducting bridge between the reference electrode electrolyte and the electrolysis electrolyte. The gel is leak proof and hence possible chlorine or halogen contamination is ruled out. Prior use, GCE was cleaned with alumina slurry of 1 μm followed by 0.3 μm, washed thoroughly with Milli-Q water and then sonicated in ethanol for few seconds to get rid of adsorbed moieties, if any and finally the cleaned GCE was surface modified with the Cu-microstructures obtained under different conditions. For this, 7 mg of the sample was suspended in a solution of 600 μL isopropyl alcohol, 200 μL water and 20 μL nafion and the mixture was sonicated for ca. 20min into a well-dispersed suspension. Then a 20 μL aliquot was hand painted on GCE, which was then dried under IR lamp for ca. 5 min. A pre-dried TBABF4 (100mM) was added into DMSO as a supporting electrolyte which was then purged with CO2 for ∼30min before performing the ECO2R.
The reaction products of ECO2R reduction were analysed by recording gas chromatograms using NUCON 5765 gas chromatography (GC) instrument and NMR peaks from the catholyte with Bruker advance 500MHz. Gaseous products obtained from 1 h long electrolysis collected at different potentials were collected in a tedlar bag fixed on top of an electrochemical cell. 1.0 mL of this collected sample was manually injected into GC injector, and the chromatograms were acquired using a serial combination of Flame Ionization Detector (FID) coupled with a mechanizer, and TCD over elution through a molecular sieve and porapak Q columns. For determination of liquid products, 0.5 mL of electrolyte was added to 0.1 mL D2O and analysed for NMR peaks.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussions
sections.text:
Broadly, the present study can be grouped into two parts. The first part has been aimed at analysing the effect of electrolysis parameters on the shape, morphology and the crystallinity of copper particles, especially towards evolution of dendritic structures and their optimization.
However, the second part of the study has been aimed at analysis of the electro-catalytic activity of the prepared dendritic microstructures towards the reduction of CO2.

sections.heading: 3.1. Synthesis and characterization of dendritic Cu/Cu2O NPs
sections.text: Anodic dissolution has been one of the commonly used approaches to prepare nanostructure electrodeposits but with stringent conditions such as highly acidic electrolyte medium with additives like sulphuric acid, acetic acid, hydrochloric acid and phosphoric acid along with high temperatures and voltages [36,44]. Here, we have used very mild conditions, including ascorbic acid as an additive and maximum bias of just 30 V at temperatures well below the boiling point of water. Similar to the citrate moieties that are commonly used as reducing as well as a stabilizing agent for metal nanoparticles, we found that ascorbic acid plays an important role, both as reducing agent as well as a stabilizer to the NPs. Besides, it also helps in facilitating the anodic dissolution of Cu at much lower applied potential, which otherwise requires very high potential in the range of 100–150 V for sacrificial dissolution of metal anodes [35,45]. Additionally, we have also studied the evolution of dendritic shapes from the primary electrolysis product species in a systematic way by varying one of the electrolysis parameters at a time while keeping all other variables unchanged. For the growth mechanism of dendrites,the temporal evolution of shape and morphology of Cu NPs was followed with the parameters for electrosynthesis held at their optimal values. Thus, this simple approach provides a straightforward strategy towards producing the optimized electrodes based on dendritic Cu NPs.

sections.heading: 3.1.1. Set I - optimizing the additive concentration
sections.text:
To study the role of ascorbic acid additives in optimizing and stabilizing the dendritic geometry, Cu/Cu2O NPs were synthesized at different concentrations of ascorbic acid in the electrodeposition bath. For indexing the crystal structure parameters and the phase of crystallization, pXRD data was recorded and analysed for the dried powder samples. Fig. 1(a) shows a stepwise overlay of the recorded pXRD pattern of the samples prepared with 25mM, 75mM, and 100mM concentrations of ascorbic acid. Peaks at 43.4° (111), 50.5° (200), 74.4° (220) and 89.9° (311) which are common in all pXRD patterns reflect
the presence of metallic Cu (0) fcc as a predominant phase in all the obtained samples (JCPDS Card Nos. 89–2838). Additionally, few lowintensity peaks at 36.4° (111), 42.2° (200), 61.4° (220) are seen in case of 25mM sample, which is attributed to the presence of Cu(I)O fcc lattice (JCPDS Card Nos. 89–2838 and 78–2076). The remarkable presence of oxide phase in case of sample obtained with 25mM ascorbic acid as compared to other samples suggest that certain minimum concentration of ascorbic acid is a must for complete reduction of Cu2+ ions generated during anodic dissolution of Cu rod. However, it is important to note here that in addition to the ascorbic acid, the applied negative bias at the deposition substrate cathode may also assist in the reduction of Cu ions as well as Cu-oxides.
The elemental composition of the prepared samples was evaluated from EDX shown in Figure SI-1 that gives an account of the percentage of copper and oxygen in these samples. The EDX analysis shows the presence of less than 11%–19% atomic percentage of oxygen in case of 75mM and 100mM samples. This suggests the formation of metallic Cu-microstructures as dominant phase and the presence of oxygen could be due to the surface oxidation of the Cu NPs electrodeposits. Comparatively, the higher oxygen content of ∼28 % was noted in case of the sample obtained with 25mM ascorbic acid, supporting the speculation that an optimum concentration of ascorbic acid is essential to get the metallic copper NPs. Moreover, the oxygen contents have been found to decrease with increasing concentration of ascorbic acid used in an electrochemical deposition bath, from 28 % (25mM) to 19 % (75mM) to 11 % (100mM) validating the role of ascorbic acid as a reducing and a stabilising agent in the present synthesis.
For morphology of the synthesized particles, the electrodeposits were subjected to FESEM and TEM imaging. The FESEM images of the samples obtained under varying concentrations of ascorbic acid (Fig. 1) suggest that the sample obtained with 25mM ascorbic acid contains mostly small-sized polygons and spherical Cu-electrodeposits that aggregate to form elongated (cone shape) microstructures, where the size of individual Cu particle vary roughly from 50 nm to 600 nm. However, the presence of a few dendrites along with a large number of smaller polygons and spherical electrodeposits was also noted as depicted by TEM image shown in Figure SI-2. Here, 25mM sample depicts presence of polygons, and few elongated particles besides self-assembled dendrite-like structures with underdeveloped branching. The sample
obtained with 75mM concentration suggest self-assembling of Cu particles into dendrite-like structures, but the samples depict large extent of agglomeration. Nevertheless, few separated underdeveloped dendrites can also be seen in the TEM image corresponding to 75mM sample. The sample obtained with 100mM ascorbic acid concentration demonstrates fully developed dendrite structures with excellent branching. Thus, the microscopic investigations establish the requirement of an optimum concentration of an organic additive for generation of Cu dendrites.
Further, to understand the effect of varying additive concentrations during electrodeposition, on the physicochemical properties of the resulting electrodeposits, we have investigated the electro-catalytic performance of these deposits toward electroreduction of CO2. Fig. 2 depicts the CV polarization curves recorded over Cu nano-dendrites (prepared at a different concentration of ascorbic acid) modified GCE in CO2 saturated DMSO. The depicted CVs are background corrected. For their background correction, the i-V responses at similar scan rates recorded over the respective electrodes in the presence of N2-purged DMSO electrolyte solution were subtracted from the similar responses recorded on the corresponding electrode using CO2 saturated DMSO electrolyte solution. This was done to nullify the contribution from capacitive current, and to enusre that the current analysed is mostly due to the ECO2R.
Cyan coloured CV curve shown in Fig. 2 (left panel) corresponds to the CV response from bare GCE (i.e. GCE without modification by Cu NPs) in the presence of CO2. As can be seen from the polarization curves, bare GCE does not show any considerable response within the tested potential range. However, the Cu-electrodeposit modified GCE shows significant current enhancement in the presence of CO2, indicating that the prepared Cu-electrodeposits are highly active electrocatalysts towards ECO2R. When GCE is modified with 25mM sample, the potential of ca. -1.2 V is required to reach the current density of -0.5 mAcm−2 which in case of 75mM sample is a little more negative, at -1.3 V. However, the polarization curve of 100mM sample requires the potential of only -1.0 V to reach the same current density, which is minimum among these three samples. Moreover, the onset potential value (less than -0.8 V) for 100mM sample is lowest among these samples, suggesting that 100mM concentration of ascorbic acid could be an optimum additive concentration for efficient electro-catalytic activity. The values of onset potential and overpotential required to reach -0.5 mAcm−2 current density along with crystalline phases as a function of electrochemical deposition parameters are summarized in Table SI-1.
The response of CV polarization curves recorded for the presented electrocatalyst materials suggest that these electrodes are highly active towards the electroreduction of CO2. To ascertain the nature of ECO2R products, we assorted to the post electrolysis GC analysis of the electrolyte solutions following the protocol mentioned in the experimental section. The details of the gas chromatography measurements along with the few representative gas chromatograms are given in Supporting information Section SI-3. Fig. 2(right panel) shows the F.E. values of the
different products electro-produced at overpotentials corresponding to faradaic current of 0.5 mA over electrocatalysts produced with varying concentrations of ascorbic acid in the electrodeposition bath. As can be noted from the figure that two (produced with 25mM and 75mM ascorbic acid) of the three tested samples show the generation of CO along with methane as major product. However, the sample prepared with 100mM of L-ascorbic acid shows presence of ethane with F.E of 29 % as the primary product and lesser production of methane with F.E. less than 6 %. Moreover, 100mM sample shows the highest activity towards ECO2R with generation of CO with F.E. of 32 % as compared to 17 % for 25mM and 13 % for 75mM samples. The production of formate is observed with all the samples as the only substantial liquid product. We tested the impact of electrolysis over potential for ECO2R wherein the trend noticed in variation in F.E. values for ECO2R to CO (see later sections of the MS) was observed to well correspond to our observations from CV polarization curves, where 100mM sample seems to exhibit the highest activity followed by 25mM sample and then least by 75mM sample. The production of ethane cannot be due to the adherent (if any) ascorbic acid as in such case ethane should be detectable in all the tested Cu electrodeposits samples (like 60 °C, 70 °C, 90 °C, 7.5 V, 15 V, 15min, 30min and 45min) which were synthesised with 100mM ascorbic acid and other varying reaction parameters. No production of ethene and any other unsaturated hydrocarbon was further confirmed via negative results from bromine water test.
The production of the methane and ethane in addition to CO during ECO2R over Cu surfaces has been predicted theoretically [46] and demonstrated experimentally as well [47,48]. It is argued that the conversion of CO2 to hydrocarbons such as methane, ethane and ethylene on Cu-surfaces involves the reduction of CO2 to CO as the first step in the formation of products. According to the Amatore− Savéant mechanism [49], the reduction of CO2 in solvents of low proton availability such as DMF, DMSO and ACN involve three competing pathways: one of the pathways consists of self-coupling of the anion radicals (CO2%−) to form oxalate whereas the other includes coupling of oxygen− carbon from CO2%− with CO2, leading to the formation of CO and carbonate. Besides these two activation pathways, protonation of CO2- by residual water followed by homogeneous electron transfer from CO2 anion radical leading to the formation of formate and hydrocarbons has also been observed for ECO2R. The key steps of the reduction process involve initial electron transfer and the rate determining steps of the three competing reactions leading to oxalate, CO, and formate. The production of methane (CH4) and ethane (C2H6) along with CO in the present study can be ascribed to the presence of residual water in DMSO electrolyte solution since DMSO is highly hygroscopic in nature and it can easily absorb moisture during transfer and handling processes. Solvent/electrolyte used in ECO2R plays an essential role in the mechanistic and kinetic aspects of the overall process. As is summarised in table SI-2, different products are reported with different electrolytes as the medium not only influences the CO2 availability but also can alter the mechanism for ECO2R.
It is important to note here that usually, C2H4 (ethylene) is observed
in greater quantity than ethane during CO2 reduction with copper structures, but in our case, the dominant product was ethane instead of ethylene. Our investigations regarding the possible production of ethylene during ECO2R over dendritic Cu electrodeposits clearly establish zero production. Hence production of ethylene via the dimerization of CO* followed by hydrogenation [29] is ruled out, as this pathway should lead to equal quantities of ethene and ethane, which is contrary to our findings. Though our studies can`t establish the exact mechanism for this preferential formation of ethane over ethylene, we hypothesize it to be on account of CH3* CH3* dimerization route predominating the CO-CO dimerization, similar to that reported by Yeo and co-workers [50] for thick oxide-derived copper catalysts. As per Yeo and co-workers [50] the higher selectivity for ethane and ethanol formation is attributed to a higher population of Cu+ sites in the thick oxide-derived Cu-films, which stabilize the –CH3 intermediate species. We presume that the dendritic structures used in our presented study probably favour the formation of ethane by stabilizing the –CH3 intermediate. However, we could not establish a direct relationship between the extent of population of Cu+ sites to the yield of ethane over these surfaces. So, we presume that in addition to the population of Cu+ sites, the morphology, as well as the crystallinity of the exposed facets (discussed later in the text) is also vital for the preferential formation of ethane.
Another important observation that we have noted in our present study is the effect of electrochemical cell design: single compartment versus two-compartment. In a two chambered custom made cell fitted with Nafion (117) membrane separating catholyte from anolyte was used to check the possible anodic interference in products of CO2 reduction. With optimized dendritic catalyst, we found that there is a mere increase of 3% in production of ethane while a small amount (i.e. 6.9 %) of ethene while increase in HER by 7% and>3% formate and 1% or less ethanol while reduction in CO production by 17 % is observed. These observations pacify the common belief that most of the CO2 reduction products are oxidized over counter electrode in a single chamber cell.
Thus, from the evaluation of the activity of the analysed additive concentrations, the Cu electrodeposit with 100mM ascorbic acid was found to be the best followed by 25mM and 75mM sample showing the lowest activity. The observed trend can be explained by taking into consideration two of the important factors related to microstructure and crystallinity of the resulting samples that vary as a function of additive concentrations. 75mM sample has aggregated dendrite shaped Cu microstructures, and hence lowest activity among the studied materials. 25mM sample is mostly made up of small-sized spherical and polygonal electrodeposit and hence expected to carry more surfaceactive sites as compared to 75mM sample. In comparison, 100mM sample shows the highest activity for CO2 reduction owing to a large number of corners and branches of dendrites seen throughout the sample.
Besides morphology, the crystallinity of the exposed facets has been found to have a profound effect on the electro-catalytic activity of the Cu electrodeposits towards ECO2R. The type of exposed facets and steps in Cu electrodeposits have been reported [51–53] to effect the product profile of CO2 reduction significantly. To explore the role of exposed facets, we calculated the ratio of (111) to (200) facet populations of Cu electrodeposits from their pXRD pattern and the estimated ratios are given in Table SI-1. The comparison of the (111) to (200) ratio suggests that for most of the materials synthesised and tested in the present investigation, the presence of (111) facets is more than (200) facets. In case of Set-I, we noticed that the XRD peak intensity ratio of (111) to (200) peaks increases from ca. 3.0 for 25mM sample to 3.21 for 100mM sample, similar to what was observed for the electro-catalytic activity of these materials. The lower electro-catalytic activity of the 75mM sample in spite of the higher (111)/(200) intensity ratio could be attributed to the presence of large aggregated structures in this sample.
The higher density of (111) exposed facets was also established via underpotential deposition of lead (Pb-UPD) investigations. UPD is a phenomenon in which a metal deposits onto a foreign substrate at potentials positive to the reversible Nernst potential or the thermodynamic equilibrium potential. When interactions between the depositing metal and the underlying substrate (M-S) are energetically more favourable than the metal-to-metal (M-M) interactions, the phenomenon of UPD is observed. The analysis of UPD is especially useful in view of the fact that (sub)monolayer formation of species on different crystal surfaces or polycrystalline metals can be employed for facet identification of exposed surfaces. The higher peak current in the UPD CV curve associated with the particular crystal facets indicates the higher population of the facet under study. Figure SI-4 shows the typical Pb-UPD CV curves recorded for different catalyst surfaces obtained under varying conditions viz — Set-I to Set-IV. A broad cathodic CV peak positioned at -0.33 to -0.35 V vs Ag/AgCl can be ascribed to the deposition of Pb on (111) facets of Cu. A closer look at these CV curves indicates that the catalyst surfaces with a dominance of (111) facets are among the most active catalysts investigated in the presented study. Thus, from the above discussion, we can conclude that the fully exposed (111) facets and the fine branching of dendrite microstructures are the most active electro-catalytic sites for ECO2R and they lead to the selective production of ethane over methane.
Besides activity, the stability of the catalyst or electro-catalyst is yet another important parameter that decides its possible utility for any kind of reaction on a commercial scale. Therefore, finally, the stability of the most active catalyst material was studied for its potential long term application towards electrochemical reduction of CO2. Figure SI-5 shows the chrono-amperogram recorded on the GCE modified with the most active catalyst (i.e. prepared at an optimized reaction parameters) immersed in DMSO electrolyte solution under continuous purging of CO2 at an applied potential of -1.0 V. As can be seen, the chrono-amperometric response of this electrode is stable even after 12 h of continuous operation without any significant decrease in its electro-catalytic activity. This suggests that the Cu nano-dendrites prepared via the present method are very stable and has the potential for long-term application and hence commercialization. Further, it is important to mention here that the application of electrode potential is known to modify the crystallinity of the electro-catalyst samples used for the electrolysis. Therefore, to check the crystalline features of the Cu microstructured electro-catalysts, the XRD patterns (figure SI-6 (a)) were recorded on the electrocatalyst samples after the CO2 electrochemical reduction. The XRD of the spent catalyst showed a minor decrease in the (111)/(200) intensity ratio from 3.21 to 3.05 for 100mM sample which suggest slight variation in the catalytic activity of the bestproven catalyst in this study. Interestingly, this decrease of (111)/(200) intensity ratio was little higher but not significant for 25mM sample where it changes from 3.0–2.72. These observations clearly establish the long term robustness of electrocatalysts synthesized in present work.
Recently, it has been shown that the molecules adsorbed on copper catalyst surface can modify the catalytic activity and selectivity towards particular products [54]. For example, modification of Cu-surfaces with poly(acrylic acid) and poly(acrylamide) via the oxygen atom on the carbonyl groups was found [54] to enhance the ethylene formation by (i) charge donation to the copper surface that activates CO for dimerization, (ii) chemical stabilization of the CO dimer (a key intermediate for C2 products) by hydrogen-bond interactions with the−NH2 group, and (iii) facilitating the adsorption of CO molecules near the polymer, increasing local surface coverage. On the other hand, poly(allylamine) was noted to completely suppress CO2 reduction activity in favour of the hydrogen evolution reaction. In the present study, we have used ascorbic acid, which may interact with Cu-surfaces with its carbonyl group(s) and may modify the catalytic properties following similar interactions. To confirm if an acid or its derived product continues to be a part of Cu-electrodeposits, the electrodeposits were subjected to XPS
analysis (Figure SI-7). This is particularly essential considering the fact that C2H6 is formed only when 100mM ascorbic acid is used for the synthesis of Cu-microstructures. From the XPS study of these samples, we found that the population of bonded -COOH is similar or rather a bit more in 25mM sample than in 100mM confirming that ascorbic acid except than controlling the morphology and crystallinity of the samples which effects the reduction of CO2 doesn’t stick to the surface of the catalyst and hence does not take part in the electro-reduction of CO2.

sections.heading: 3.1.2. Set II- optimizing the applied voltage
sections.text:
After analysing the effect of additive concentration, we investigated the role of deposition potential over the morphology and electrocatalytic activity of Cu-electrodeposits. Similar to the Set-I, materials obtained at different applied voltage viz. 7.5 V, 15 V and 30 V were analysed for their crystalline and lattice properties. Fig. 3(a) shows an overlay of XRD pattern recorded on the samples prepared at 7.5 V, 15 V and 30 V of applied voltage. Peaks at 43.4°, 50.5°, 74.4° and 89.9° respectively correspond to (111), (200), (220) and (311) planes of fcc lattice of metallic copper as suggested by JCPDS Card No. 89-2838. EDX spectra (Fig. SI-8) suggests the presence of majority of copper in all three samples (with 10–13 % of atomic oxygen), which confirms the presence of metallic Cu in the majority. However, as mentioned earlier, traces of native oxide layer are also evident on the surface of Cu NPs.
FESEM image of the 7.5 V sample (Fig. 3b and c) shows that small dendrites are stationed on the polygons (beneath the dendrites). It seems that as if these dendrites have been evolved from the polygonal edges through protrusion where all dendrites have not grown in synchronization. On the other hand, FESEM image of the sample prepared at 15 V (Fig. 3d) depicts the morphology as that of the colony of corals, emerging from a base with radial branching. However, as described in Set-I, the sample prepared at 30 V shows fully developed dendrite structures with fine branching. TEM images (Fig. SI-9) also demonstrate that 30 V applied voltage generates the finely branched dendritic Cu microstructures. Fig. 3(e) shows the polarization CV curves recorded on GCE modified with Cu NPs prepared at varying bias voltages. The sample prepared at 7.5 V comprised of smaller dendrites stationed on polygons and shows good activity for CO2 reduction, harbouring
overpotential of -1.22 V to reach -0.5mA/cm² of current density. As already discussed in FESEM analysis, 15 V sample has a much better population of dendrites than that of 7.5 V sample, hence as predicted its catalytic activity is better than the sample obtained at 7.5 V applied potential. However, 30 V sample is best among these samples in terms of the quality of dendritic structure such as presence of extensive primary and secondary branches, and hence it has the best activity for CO2 reduction with lowest overpotential (-1.0 V) required to reach a current density of -0.5 mA/cm². The analysis of the CO2 reduction reaction product ascertains the formation of CO and methane in all the samples. Interestingly, the F.E. corresponding to the formation of methane decreases from 29 % (7.5 V sample) to< 5% (30 V sample), but the F.E. for ethane formation increases from negligible (7.5 V sample) to 29 % (30 V sample) for the samples obtained with increasing applied voltages. Moreover, the sample obtained with 30 V of applied voltage during electrochemical deposition was found to convert CO2 to CO with largest F.E. (i.e. 33 %) as compared to the other samples prepared at different voltages.
The trend in variation of ECO2R activity analysed from CV polarization curves as well as F.E. values suggest that the selective formation of ethane over methane strongly depends on the morphology of the samples. Besides, the electro-catalytic activity of these materials was also observed to be dependent on the intensity ratio of (111) to (200) XRD peaks. The sample prepared at 7.5 V depicts (111)/(200) intensity ratio of 2.71, however, the sample prepared at 30 V shows it to be 3.21. Higher the (111)/(200) intensity ratio, higher is the conversion efficiency to ethane. The trend in variation of F.E. values for methane follows exactly opposite than that of ethane, here lower the (111)/ (200) intensity ratio higher is the F.E. for ethane. These observations also confirm that the morphology, along with the crystallinity of the Cucatalyst plays a deciding role in determining their catalytic activity.

sections.heading: 3.1.3. Set III- optimizing the reaction temperature
sections.text:
After optimizing the concentration of additive and bias voltage, we tried to explore the effect of temperature viz. 60 °C, 70 °C, 80 °C and 90 °C for the synthesis of dendritic Cu electrodeposits. The morphology of materials prepared under different temperatures was analysed under
FESEM imaging like the previous two sets, and the samples were also found to consist of dendrites and polygons. As shown in Fig. 4, sample prepared at 60 °C shows a mixture of both polygons and dendrites, where the population of polygons is more than the dendrites. The sample prepared at 70 °C shows more dendrites and lesser polygons as compared to 60 °C sample, but the polygons are appearing with their edges covered by the deposited particles. It suggests that the dendrite formation initiates on the edges of polygons in the form of protrusions, which then finally transforms into the dendrites. Same was the case with 60 °C sample where polygons are more in number indicating that this temperature may not be sufficient for its transformation into the dendrites.
As mentioned earlier, the sample obtained at 80 °C consists of dendritic structures with extensive branching, as shown in Fig. 1(d). However, further increasing the electrodeposition temperature to 90 °C, this branching is found to deteriorate somehow, and coral reef type of morphology was seen instead of dendrite branching. Similar observations are also noted from TEM images (Figure SI-10) recorded on these samples prepared at different temperatures. Overall, 80 °C temperature is found to be the optimum to generate the dendritic Cu microstructures with better homogeneity and extensive branching. The samples prepared at different reaction temperatures were further analysed for their lattice properties by recording XRD pattern, as shown in Fig. 4(d). All the XRD patterns shows the peaks at 43.4°, 50.5°, 74.4° and 89.9° corresponding to (111), (200), (220) and (311) planes of fcc crystalline structure of metallic copper (JCPDS Card No. 89-2838) along with a low intensity peak at 37° related to Cu(I) oxide that could have been formed due to the surface oxidation of metallic copper. Elemental detection by EDS (Fig. SI-11) was done on these samples, and it was found that the spectrum shows peaks for copper (most intense) and oxygen (less intense) suggesting metallic copper as major component in the prepared samples.
The samples prepared at different temperatures were also tested for their electro-catalytic activity towards ECO2R. Fig. 5 (left panel) shows the CV polarization curves for CO2 reduction using electrodes modified with the samples prepared at different electrodeposition temperatures. All the materials show electro-catalytic activity towards the reduction of CO2, where sample prepared at 80 °C shows the highest activity in terms of lowest onset potential and highest current density. 60 °C sample harbours overpotential of -1.55 V for -0.5 mA/cm² of current density whereas 70 °C sample required an overpotential of -1.53 V to
reach the same current density. As further, the morphology improves in case of 80 °C sample, overpotential requirement decreases to –1.0 V for –0.5 mA/cm² current density. As expected from the deteriorated dendritic morphology of the Cu NPs prepared at 90 °C, the electro-catalytic activity towards CO2 reduction is less as compared to 80 °C sample harbouring overpotential of -1.48 V to reach the current density of -0.5 mA/cm2. Moreover, the 80 °C sample shows highest F.E. for CO2 conversion to ethane as compared to the other samples, whereas the F.E. for methane increases with the increase in the temperature employed for the synthesis of Cu-electro-deposit, except 80 °C sample that shows lowest conversion efficiency for methane.

sections.heading: 3.1.4. Set-IV: optimizing the reaction time for the evolution of dendrites
sections.text:
Based on the results from the above three sets, it was noted that dendritic shapes with a larger number of edges and corners are found to be more active. Also, it was conjectured that dendrite morphology might have been evolved from the edges of polygons. Thus, to further ascertain the growth mechanism, temporal evolution of shapes was studied at different reaction time intervals, while keeping rest three of the electrodeposition parameters constant as optimized in the previous sets.
Different samples for 10min, 15min, 30min, 40min, 45min and 60min electrodeposiion were prepared and explored via FESEM and TEM imaging for up shooting their morphology. Fig. 6 shows the FESEM images of the materials synthesised for six different elecectrodeposition time intervals. One can notice that 10min sample shows the presence of only polygons with varying sizes in the range from 1.0 μm to 1.5 μm. When the electro-deposition time was increased to 15min, we noted that these polygons grow in size along with clearly exposed distinct edges that were not evident in case of the sample obtained at 10min. of electro-deposition. Further increment in electrodeposition time to 30min leads to further enhancement in the polygon number density. Besides, the edges of polygons are found to get covered with smaller Cu NPs while their faces remain uncovered. This could be due to the higher surface energy of the facets than the faces. The samples obtained at 40min. demonstrate that besides edges the faces of polygons also get covered with spherical Cu particles. However, few elongated structures emerging from the growth of Cu NPs are also seen for this reaction time interval. On further increment in the electro-deposition time to 45min, FESEM image shows more of an agglomerated polygon with larger protrusions. Nevertheless, the presence of an
occasional porous network of polygons is also seen in the FESEM image. For 60min electro-deposition time we found that there are more of dendrites with very few agglomerated spherical Cu particles and polygons. Presence of one-dimensional structure along with dendrites can be noticed while taking a close look at the images of 60min sample suggesting that the dendrite is made of monomer joints. So, we could conclude that the growth of dendrites occurs via deposition of material on the edges of polygons which undergo further growth through protrusion. TEM images shown in Fig. SI-12 further supports the growth mechanism of dendrites from polygonal edges. TEM image for 40min sample display just an initiation of the growth of side branches on the elongated shaft that further grows into dendrites at 45min. However, the number density of dendrites is very less in case of 45min sample than the sample obtained post 60min of electro-deposition.
Fig. 7 (left panel) shows an overlay of the XRD pattern recorded over six samples prepared for varied electro-deposition time interval viz. 10min, 15min, 30min, 40min, 45min and 60min. All the samples display peaks at 43.4°, 50.5°, 74.4° and 89.9° that correspond to (111), (200), (220) and (311) planes of fcc lattice of metallic copper. Smaller peaks at 37° and 63° in some of the samples correspond to (111) and (220) planes of fcc lattice of copper (I) oxide. Elemental analysis by EDX spectroscopy (Fig. SI-13) was also done on the samples and peaks for
copper (most intense), and oxygen (minor) were noticed in all the samples.
Further, to validate the structure-property relationship, we tested these samples for their electro-catalytic potential toward ECO2R. The 10min sample requires a potential of -1.5 V for -0.5 mA/cm² current density, which is most negative among the tested samples and thus implying its lowest activity. In the case of 15min sample, this potential requirement is shifted to -1.2 V for -0.5 mA/cm² current density. This increase in activity can be attributed to the exposure of edges from the polygons. In 30min sample, the activity decreased again as the edges that were highly active as found in 15min sample are now covered with the spherical Cu particles (refer to TEM images). The required potential shifted negatively from -1.2 V to -1.25 V for 30min sample to reach the same current density. This trend proves that more the number of edges or corners better is the surface for catalysis. In 40min sample, the polygons are now covered along with edges (refer TEM image) hence lesser surface is exposed which causes activity to decrease along with negative shift in potential from -1.25 V for 30min sample to -1.52 V for 40min sample. Analysing 45min sample for CO2 reduction, we found that it is better than 40min sample and this may be because of presence of some dendrites in its structure. Finally, 60min sample was tested for CO2 reduction, and as mentioned earlier, its activity was found best
among all the samples with the requirement of potential as low as -1.0 V to reach -0.5mA/cm² current density which can be attributed to the presence of extensive branching in the dendrites.
Furthermore, F.E from the gas chromatography analysis (depicted in Figure SI-14) of the CO2 reduction reaction products suggest that the sample obtained after 60min of electro-deposition exhibits the best electro-catalytic CO2 reduction activity by exhibiting 32 % FE for CO in comparison to 20 % produced by the sample obtained after 15min of electro-deposition that shows the second best activity among the investigated samples. The sample obtained after just 10min of electrochemical deposition does not show the detectable quantity of any gaseous products which is in accordance with the corresponding CV polarization curve that does not show appreciable current associated with the ECO2R. Again, the trend in the quantity of CO produced as a function of electrochemical deposition time matches well with the CV polarization curves, where samples obtained at 60min and 15min shows respectively the best and second-best activity followed by the samples electrodeposited for 30min and 45min. The sample obtained after 40min of electro-deposition shows the lowest activity. The methane produced by these samples also varies in the same order where the F.E. for methane has been noted to decrease continuously with increasing electro-deposition time interval, except for 45min sample. Table SI-1 summarises comparison of crystalline properties, exposed facets, overpotential and their effect on overall faradaic efficiency.

sections.heading: 3.2. Plausible mechanism of dendrite formation
sections.text:
The above-discussed observations point towards two important inferences (1) the dendritic shapes evolve from the polygons, which in turn are produced in-situ by the reduction of Cu2+ ions (obtained by anodic dissolution of Cu rod) in the presence of L-ascorbic acid and (2) a minimum concentration of L-Ascorbic acid as well as other parameters such as electrodeposition time is essential for the evolution of dendrites from the polygons. For example, as discussed in section 3.1D related to the optimization of the reaction time for the evolution of dendrites, it was found that initially (at 10min) only spherical shaped Cu electrodeposits are obtained which then grow into the shape of polygons after 15min of electrodeposition. Similarly, when the additive concentration was varied while keeping all other electrodeposition parameters (time, temperature and voltage) constant, the sample obtained with 25mM of Ascorbic acid as an additive leads only to the spherical electrodeposits which get transformed into polygons for 75mM of the additive and finally taking the shape of dendrites for presence of 100mM of Ascorbic acid. This further highlights the crucial role played by additives used during the electrochemical deposition. Thus, based on these observations, we propose followed plausible mechanism for the evolution of dendritic Cu electrodeposits in the present study (Scheme 1).
Anodic dissolution and corrosion of copper from pure copper metals
and alloys have been studied widely in the past, and the rate of anodic dissolution is known to be highly dependent on species present in the solution. It has been shown that ascorbic acid has the special potential to act as corrosion inhibitor as well as an activator for corrosion/dissolution processes [40]. It is also a well-known fact that Cu dissolution may take place in uni- and bi-valent states as per following reactions,
Cu → Cu2+ + 2e− (1)
Cu → Cu1+ + e− (2)
Reaction (1) has been reported to be the dominant one as Cu1+ species are not as stable as Cu2+. Thus, obtained Cu bivalent ions can undergo one of the following two reactions, based upon the solution conditions.
Cu2+ + 2e− → Cuo (3)
Cu2+ + 2OH− → Cu (OH)2 (4)
In the present case, reaction (3) could be predominant as the resulting product is majority of metallic copper. Metallic copper formed by reaction (3) may also undergo oxidation with oxygen (either from dissolved in solution or from air) leading to the formation of traces of Cu2O (reaction 5).
4Cu+O2 → 2Cu2O (5)
The Cuo nuclei formed in reaction (3) would undergo crystal growth along the faces with higher surface tension which eventually disappear from the final appearance, leaving low-energy surfaces exposed as per the Gibbs-Wulff’s theorem [55,56]. Skriver et al. [57] with the help of simulation results reported that in case of copper, among the three basic facets of {100}, {111}, and {110}, {110} exhibits the lowest work function and the highest surface energy. Therefore, the copper crystal growth rate increases progressively along the< 111 > ,< 100 > , and< 110>directions, which is determined by the relative order of the surface energies. However, when organic additives such as Ascorbic acid is present during the crystal growth process, the relative order of the surface energies can get modified. The preferential adsorption of an additive can lower the surface energy of the bound planes and thus hinders the growth of a crystal towards the direction which is perpendicular to this plane [56] and hence the final morphology of the crystal may change.
Electrodeposition method besides being simple and low cost provides the possibility of controlling the shape or crystallographic orientation of the nuclei by changing the associated parameter such as pH, temperature, applied potential and solution precursors or additives [58–61]. Xue et al. [55] studied crystallization behaviour and formation mechanism of dendrite Cu2O crystals which follow the similar trend as that of cubic Cuo with respect to the surface energies and work functions along the different crystalline faces. They have shown that the morphology evolution takes place due to the enhancement of the
transfer of Cu2+ through stirring the electrolyte solution and the elimination of the Cu2+ depletion zone around the nuclei that promotes the deposition of copper atoms along the close-packed, i.e. < 110> direction in order to minimize the system energy and thus, to form fcc Cu lattice crystal under a cathodic potential. As a result of this type of growth, the morphology of the Cu2O crystals develops into dendrites, and the growth direction of the dendrites remain all along the<110 >directions. Similar observations are also reported by McShane et al. [58] while making the Cu2O photoactive electrodes composed of dendritic crystals produced via electrochemical deposition using acetate buffer solution with slightly acidic pH. Moreover, they have reported that the acetate ions help in maintaining the pH near the working electrode regardless of the deposition rate, which is essential for transforming and maintaining the thermodynamically unstable morphologies like branches and dendrites. The bottom line of all these studies is that the dendritic branching growth in electrodeposition can be induced by increasing the deposition rate to form a depletion zone of the nutrient ions (i.e., Cu2+ for Cu deposition) around a growing crystal and by controlling the pH near the electrode.
In the present study, we have noticed that the formation of dendritic morphology is favoured by increasing the concentration of ascorbic acid additive, reaction temperature and applied voltage. Incidentally, all these parameters can contribute to the enhancement of transportation of nutrient ions and thus to the elimination of depletion region around the nuclei, hence favours the growth of Cu electrodeposits in dendritic morphology. Furthermore, the ascorbic acid that ionizes as ascorbate ion above pH of 5 may act similar to the acetate ions in controlling the pH near the electrode surface and thus may further assist in transforming dendrite morphology. Similar to the results of McShame et al. we also noticed that the increase in the ascorbic acid concentration from 25mM to 75mM to 100mM leads to the enhancement in the number density of dendritic Cu microstructures. Such an increase in the number density of Cu microstructures with dendritic morphology can be expected due to enhancement in the nucleation density with increase in ascorbate ion concentration because the higher ascorbic acid concentration could result into shift in the reduction of potential (Ered) of Cu2+ ions to the less negative potential, similar to acetate ions [61]. To check whether such kind of shift in reduction potential of Cu2+ would occur due to the increase in ascorbic acid concentration (in the present case), we recorded the CV curves on the solution containing varying ascorbic acid concentration. Fig. 8 clearly shows the shift in Ered of Cu2+ towards more positive/lower negative potential with increased concentration of ascorbic acid. This shift is maximum for 100mM ascorbic acid concentration. Thus, all those parameters that increase the nucleation density, such as applied potential, temperature, the concentration of ascorbic acid, would help in generating dendrite morphology.
Similar observations have been noted by Wang et al. [62] in the case of crystal growth on the surfaces of Cu polygons with different facets, where it has been shown that the growth is faster on the edges of polygons thereby resulting in the exposure of low-energy surfaces. Further, they have shown that Cu nanocrystals with enriched high-energy {110} facets showed significantly enhanced activity toward CO2 reduction. In the same line, we could expect the formation of dendrite structures taking place with the growth of Cu particles at the edges of polygons.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we show that ascorbic acid plays an important role as an additive in the synthesis of dendritic copper microstructures via electrodeposition. It not only acts as a stabilizer to control the growth of copper into nano-dimension but also assists in electro-dissolution of the copper rod, which otherwise requires a very high DC voltage and stringent experimental conditions. Further, we show that the shape and morphology of Cu electrodeposit determines their activity for ECO2R. The edges and corners of Cu electrodeposit (both, dendrites and polygons) are more effective catalyst sites than the smooth surfaces. The higher activity of the fully exposed branches of dendrites can be attributed to the enrichment of the high-energy facets. Furthermore, the growth pattern of the Cu NPs prepared following simple, green electrolysis approach was studied in detail and evolution of dendritic structured Cu microstructures were optimized with respect to several electrolysis parameters, and was noted that the evolution of dendrites takes place from simple polygons which are formed at the early stage of electrolysis.
